title: Standard Form 1: Converting
summary: Why we use standard form, and converting large and small numbers both ways. Large numbers: two methods (one step, or one ten at a time). Small numbers: write the first number between 1 and 10, then divide by a power of ten. The place value grid then gives the quicker rule (down a place, power up 1). Numbers in parts come last of all. Whiteboards have five questions and no hints. Printed Sheets 1 and 2 are placeholders. All questions are authored.

els.text: Why we use it, and converting
Write large and small numbers in standard form, and convert them back.

•  Say why standard form is used
•  Say whether a number is in standard form
•  Convert large and small numbers both ways

Your calculator switches to it when the answer will not fit on the screen.

A number is in standard form when it is written as

$A \times 10^{n}$

where $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ is an integer.

slides.title: Is it in standard form?

slides.title: Laws of indices: four quick ones

els.text: Laws of indices: four quick ones
The law the small-number method uses: one over a power of ten is a negative power.

slides.title: Small numbers: divide by tens
slides.brief: Model 1: a decimal is a number between 1 and 10 divided by a power of ten, and the laws of indices turn the division into a negative power.

slides.title: Get it between 1 and 10 first
slides.brief: Model 2: two digits. Write the digits as a number between 1 and 10 (3.5) and divide by 10, rather than 35 ÷ 100 and then fixing it.

slides.title: More zeros
slides.brief: Model 3: five decimal places but the power is -4. The power is not the number of zeros: it is how many tens we divide 5.8 by.

els.text: We divided by tens, so the number is smaller than 1. A number smaller than 1 has a negative power.

els.text:
•  Standard form is $A \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ an integer.
•  Large: write the number as $A$ times a 1 with zeros, then as a power of ten; or peel off one ten at a time.
•  Small: write $A$, divide by a power of ten, and the power is negative.
•  Down one place, the power goes up by $1$. Up one place, the power goes down by $1$.
